title: TB8-17391
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is citizen of Grenada who came to Canada in 1999. He made a refugee claim in February 2013. It was refused by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) and he appealed to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).
The appeal is allowed. The matter is referred back to the RPD to be redetermined because the Appellant should have had a Designated Representative (DR).

At the time of the June 28, 2018 hearing, the Appellant was affected by illness that impaired his cognitive ability. Relevant evidence or argument in support of his claim may not have been adequately provided as a result and thus the RAD cannot rely on the RPD Record to decide the appeal.
The referral back is not an instruction to allow or to dismiss the claim. If the RAD could allow or dismiss the appeal on the merits, it would do so.
The lack of a DR at the time of the RPD hearing is a procedural defect that cannot be cured by the merit-based RAD process, as explained in this decision.
The claim should be heard by a different panel if possible.
If the Appellant's medical situation is different at the time of the redetermination, it is open to the RPD to decide that the Appellant does not require a DR.

In 2009, the Appellant was involved in an incident in Canada that generated charges of murder and manslaughter against him. In 2012, he was acquitted. He made a refugee claim in February 2013. He claims that relatives of the two deceased victims will harm or kill him if he is returned to Grenada.

The claim has a lengthy history. It was refused by an RPD Member on May 7, 2015 but on appeal, the RAD returned the matter to the RPD for redetermination because a change in the legislation meant that the RPD member who decided the case did not have authority to make the decision.

A different RPD Member refused the claim on July 4, 2018 after a new hearing. The RPD Member evaluated the country evidence and concluded that there is state protection in Grenada for the Appellant if he should need it.

A primary argument for this appeal to the RAD is a breach of procedural fairness by the RPD because it should have appointed a DR for the Appellant.1 Other arguments are about alleged errors in the RPD decision.

At the request of the Counsel representing the Appellant in this appeal, a DR was appointed by the RAD on December 11, 2018. It is not evident from the information before me that this DR has been involved in the appeal process. The Appellant is represented by Counsel who has provided the Appellant Record with new evidence and the appeal submissions.

I find that there was a breach of procedural fairness at the RPD that requires the matter to be referred back for redetermination by the RPD. PROCEDURAL FAIRNESS The matter is referred back for re-determination because of a breach of procedural fairness.
The Appellant's Counsel submits that the RPD should have appointed a DR and that this breach of procedural fairness "is determinative of the appeal".2

Counsel does not specify the appropriate remedy upon finding such a breach. Elsewhere in the arguments, the Appellant's Counsel correctly suggests that the RAD should intervene and substitute a determination or, if unable to do so, should refer the matter back for re-determination.3 To be clear, it would be incorrect to find that the Appellant is a refugee because of a breach of procedural fairness in the RPD's process. A procedural defect is remedied either by referring the matter back to the original decision-making body or through a merit-based appeal determination that cures the identified defect.

Despite the RAD's role as an independent merit-based appeal,4 the RAD is generally limited to considering the evidence in the RPD Record.5 If the Appellant was impaired such that he could not adequately prepare and present his claim to the RPD, its Record may be deficient and the RAD cannot fairly rely on it. Allowing for new evidence and an oral hearing at the RAD does not cure that type of defect because of statutory limits on the evidence that may be presented to the RAD and its limited ability to enquire into and gather evidence.6
The RPD Member found that the Appellant's concerns about what might happen in Grenada were speculative and that, in any event, the Appellant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection.

The onus was on the Appellant to show that Grenada cannot protect him from the alleged persecution or harm. I agree with the Appellant's Counsel that on these points the Appellant's ability to present his case was affected by his impaired mental capacity.

The ability to present evidence about whether the state is capable of protecting him from alleged persecution or harm, including to show the effect of and an objective basis for his fear, was critically relevant in this case. The audio record of June 28, 2018 indicates that the Appellant was able to convey evidence about his personal circumstances and subjective fear, but that he may have been impaired in understanding how to present information and arguments to rebut the presumption that Grenada can provide adequate protection or to demonstrate why adequate state protection is not available. The Appellant required a designated representative at the RPD

Even though the RPD Member conducted a thorough inquisitorial process, including with two PHCs to assist the Appellant, the RPD Member failed to recognize that, at the third sitting when the hearing proceeded, the Appellant's ability to present his case was impaired and he required a DR.

There were three in-person sittings at the RPD. The first sitting on March 1, 2018 was adjourned but the Member conducted what was, in essence, a pre-hearing conference (PHC) with the Appellant to explain the RPD process and address the Appellant's arguments about mental challenges. The RPD Member confirmed that state protection was the main issue for the claim, gave the Appellant copies of documents, including country information about state protection, explained the type of evidence that would be examined for the claim and reviewed the Appellant's medical problems. The RPD Member adjourned to give the Appellant time to seek representation and to obtain medical information that explained how his medical problems might interfere with the ability to present evidence or participate in the proceeding on his own.

During the 23-minute PHC on March 1, 2018, there was extensive discussion, note-taking by the Appellant, and repeated explanations from the RPD Member to ensure understanding. The Member also confirmed the contents of the RPD file and gave the Appellant copies of the Personal Information Form (PIF) and country information documents.

At the next sitting on April 9, 2018, the same RPD Member effectively conducted another PHC. The session lasted for 15 minutes. The RPD Member repeated what had happened at the previous PHC, explained the process again, identified the need for relevant documents and the Appellant's right to Counsel, including the possibility of legal aid. The Appellant explained that after the previous PHC he had called for an appointment with the neurologist and the earliest available was XXXX XXXX, 2018. The Appellant expected to obtain information about his mental capacity for the RPD process and the RPD Member fairly adjourned the hearing until after the neurologist appointment.

The Appellant's Counsel relies on administrative notes about these first two PHC sessions and suggests that the Appellant has no recollection of the April 9, 2018 hearing.7 I have listened to the audio transcripts of first two sittings and find that the RPD fairly assessed that the Appellant understood his responsibilities and correctly relied on the Appellant's understanding at that time. The Appellant was present, understood the RPD Member's information, presented his own evidence about the medical issues he was having in the past year, and advised the RPD Member about his upcoming neurological appointment. The Appellant presented XXXX, XXXX and XXXX 2017 medical documents about recent viral XXXX and treatment at the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and the Member correctly declined to make any medical determinations he was not qualified to make from the that evidence. Rather, the RPD Member gave the Appellant an opportunity to get an appropriate medical letter that spoke to his limitations. Throughout these two processes, the Appellant conveyed his understanding and the ability to present his case.

It is the Appellant's capacity at the third sitting, when his claim was heard, that raises concerns. A letter was presented from Dr. XXXX, XXXX, at the third sitting on June 28, 2018. It includes this assessment: [The Appellant] has XXXX XXXX and the Mini-Mental status today scoring a XXXX out of 30 with difficulty in registering information. His examination does not show any focality aside from mild gait instability but he remains fully ambulatory and independent. Due consideration of this should be given in his ability to answer for himself and for any legal matters.

Even though the RPD Member was politely considerate throughout the June 28, 2018 hearing and helpfully inquisitorial, there was evidence before him that, at that time, the Appellant needed a DR. My careful assessment of the hearing recording reflects that the unrepresented Appellant struggled to respond to questions and to present his case. There is a notable difference between the Appellant's responsiveness and coherence during the two PHCs and at the hearing on June 28, 2018, where he struggled at times, particularly when called on to explain and present evidence related to the state protection and IFA questions. He seemed affected by some cognitive deficiencies that are consistent with what is indicated in Dr. XXXX letter about difficulty registering information. In the absence of Counsel, it was the RPD's responsibility to identify that the Appellant required a DR.8 DECISION The RPD decision is set aside and the matter is returned to the RPD to be redetermined. (signed) M. Kingma M. Kingma August 3, 2020 Date 1 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), S.C. 2001, c. 27., s. 167(2): Representation. 2 Exhibit P-2, Appellant Record, Appellant's Memorandum, para. 45. 3 Exhibit P-2, Appellant Record, Appellant's Memorandum, paras. 13 and 14. 4 Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93 (CanLII) [2016] 4 FCR 157, and 2016 FCA 93. 5 It is generally anticipated that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) will make decisions based on the evidence that was presented to the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) ss.110(3) and not admit new evidence. Exceptions allowed by ss. 110(4) of the IRPA are for evidence that arose after, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been expected to have been presented at the time the claim was rejected. 6 The RAD has these options: to confirm the RPD determination; to set aside the RPD determination and substitute its own, or to refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination if it cannot make a new decision without hearing evidence that was presented to the RPD [IRPA s. 111]. 7 Exhibit P-2, Appellant Record, Appellant's Memorandum, para. 23. 8 IRPA, S.C. 2001, c. 27., s. 167(2): Representation, and (RPD) Rules, SOR/2012-256, s. 20(1): Designated Representatives: Duty of counsel or officer to notify. --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------ RAD File / Dossier de la SAR : TB8-17391 RAD.25.02 (January, 2020) Disponible en franþais 2 Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada Refugee Appeal Division Commission de l'immigration et du statut de rÚfugiÚ du Canada Section d'appel des rÚfugiÚs RAD.25.02 (January, 2020) Disponible en franþais
